title: Grom and the Whispering Mountain
markdown:
The northern reaches were a place the wind used as a workshop, twisting peaks into shapes that winked at the clouds. Snow passes gleamed like polished bone. Pine-dark valleys kept their sunlight to themselves. Tiny villages clung to cliff faces as if they had grown there on purpose.

In one such village, Crag’s Perch, nestled like a robin’s egg on a lofty shelf, lived an ogre named Grom. His dwelling sat on the outskirts, where the path gave up being a path and became an opinion. He was built like a well-rooted oak, and his heart was as decent as a summer day. Most folk expected ogres to grunt and stomp and laugh until the rafters shook. Grom preferred the quiet company of his jackdaw, Riddle. Riddle’s feathers held an iridescent black that hinted at hidden depths, and their eyes were polished obsidian with a knowing glint. They perched on Grom’s broad shoulder, a chirping shadow, and their observations cut through his silences like a pebble skipping a still pond.

The problem in Crag’s Perch was persistent. Avalanches. Every winter the mountains threatened to shed their snowy blankets onto the homes. When the snow grew deep and the mountain began to groan, the villagers called upon the Ogre of the Crag to perform the ancient Sky-Soothing Spell. Chanting that echoed through the valleys. Shimmering dust in moonlight. A small controlled burst of elemental colour. Tradition, recited with hushed reverence.

Grom had a different idea, brewing in a head more interested in stone than clouds. Practical language. Timber. Well-placed supports.

“It’s the snowpack,” he rumbled to Riddle, low thunder in the chest. “It needs to be guided, not charmed. Understood, not appeased with pretty lights.”

Under that rumble sat a quieter worry: that competence would look ordinary. That the village, hungry for the grand and the legendary, would take his grounded work for a lack of insight. The worry made him hesitate, which was annoying, because hesitation did not shore up a ridge.

The elders approached at last, faces etched with worry as deep as ravines. Elder Borin’s beard was frosted white.

“Ogre Grom,” he implored, “the snows are too heavy this year. The mountain groans. You must cast the Sky-Soothing Spell, as is tradition.”

Grom’s massive hands clenched, not in anger. Expectation sat on him like a cloak that did not fit.

“Elder Borin,” he said, steady even while unease prickled, “I don’t think a spell is what we need. The snow is unstable above the Great Ridge. If we could shore it up, channel the wind differently, perhaps with a few well-placed windbreaks, it would be far more reliable.” He pointed with a calloused finger toward the teetering places.

Elder Borin’s brow furrowed. “Grom, we respect your strength. But the Sky-Soothing Spell is more than timbers. It’s hope. It’s what our ancestors have always done, and what our hearts need to see. Mere timbers and stones won’t stir the mountain’s heart.”

The other elders nodded, polite and unmovable.

And so Grom found himself in the unfamiliar work of convincing people that the mundane might be wiser than a mountain. He spent days, Riddle fluttering overhead, studying the mountain’s moods. Wind patterns. Capricious drifts. The grain of rock that would hold. At dawn the snow looked innocent. By noon it had ideas. He collected sturdy timbers, felled with care, bark still smelling of resin, and began a reinforced barrier along the most precarious stretch of the Great Ridge. He worked without an audience, which suited him. Villagers watched from a distance, waiting for shimmer, and went home disappointed when there was only an ogre with a mallet. He nudged massive stones into place, making subtle channels that might coax the wind to whisper around the snowpack rather than roar over it. His palms split. He bound them and kept going. Riddle let out a sharp inquisitive squawk now and then, which Grom took as a reminder to keep his hands moving.

“Are you quite sure about this, Grom?” Riddle croaked at last, landing on his shoulder. “It lacks a certain flair. No shimmering lights. No grand pronouncements.”

Grom sighed, wind in a cave. “Flair doesn’t stop avalanches, Riddle. Solid wood and good sense do.”

Even as he said it, a smaller voice asked whether the elders were right, whether some magical element lived only in the spell. His hands faltered. The urge to mimic something theatrical tugged. He did not stop building. He did want to.

The sky darkened with a swiftness that felt personal. Fat snowflakes, thicker, faster. A low rumble, deeper than thunder, from the peaks. A section of the Great Ridge began to shift, a slow slide that made the ground tremble.

“It’s starting,” a villager cried.

Pale faces below. People shuffling backwards, eyes on the snow.

Grom ran. Powerful legs churning. Snow to the knee, then higher. He saw a massive boulder, dislodged, teetering above a group who had gathered to watch, frozen by the spectacle, as if watching were a kind of help.

“No,” Grom roared, plea and command together. He threw himself forward, a shield. Braced his shoulder against groaning stone. Grinding rock. Biting wind. Snow in his eyes. Disturbed soil, wet and mineral. Bones protesting. The mountain trying, quite sincerely, to crush him. For a fraction of a second the old worry flared: they would see him fail. Then he pushed, and kept pushing, until pushing was the only thought left in him.

The boulder shuddered to a halt. Snow packed against his cheek, cold as a slap. The smaller slide, diverted by his hidden channels and this unglamorous brace of brute force, flowed harmlessly down an uninhabited slope, a white river that had been talked out of the village. The villagers looked up at Grom, still a statue against the rock, breath ragged, face streaked with snow and sweat. They did not see a failed magician. They saw someone who had not let go.

The danger passed. Grom, stiff and sore, a map of aches, made his way back to his quiet dwelling on the outskirts. Riddle rode the last stretch in silence, which was a kindness. The work had been unseen until it was not. Lives had been saved. That night someone left a loaf at his door, still warm. The villagers, awed and grateful, still spoke of a miracle, of a mountain that had chosen to relent, as if the earth itself had decided to be polite. Grom, with Riddle a warm weight on his shoulder, just nodded. He had paid in strain and a lingering ache. He had paid it willingly. He slept sitting up, because lying down made the shoulder argue.

Weeks later, the first significant snowfall of the new season arrived, a soft silent descent. Barely enough to cover the pathways. Smoke from Crag’s Perch rose straight, which meant the wind was behaving. A tiny cascade, no larger than a rabbit’s hop, broke from a high ledge. Grom tensed. A phantom twinge in the shoulder. Then he watched. The snow tumbled harmlessly, melting before it reached the village. Riddle let out a soft knowing coo. Pine shadows striped the paths. Grom’s smile was unforced. The fear of being misunderstood was still a whisper. It was no longer a roar. The ridge held, timber and stone and an ogre’s stubborn shoulder. That was the part he loved, though he did not say so out loud, even to Riddle, who already knew.
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
